newsitem.title: USA: Seagram/Viacom cable dispute now in judge's hands.
newsitem.headline: Seagram/Viacom cable dispute now in judge's hands.

text.p: Seagram Co Ltd and Viacom Inc fired a last legal salvo at each other on Friday before leaving the fate of their USA Networks cable-television partnership in the hands of a Delaware judge.

Vice Chancellor Myron Steele of the Delaware Chancery Court ruled on May 15 that Viacom's MTV Networks cable operations violated a non-compete provision of the USA Networks agreement, which Viacom inherited when it acquired Paramount Communications Inc, Seagram's original partner.
But rather than imposing a remedy immediately, Steele set a 45-day cooling-off period to allow the companies agree on a single proposal or offer separate plans for his consideration.
In court papers Friday, Seagram restated its assertion that the standard remedy for a breach of contract is for a court to impose an injunction ordering the offending party to stop the violation.

"The practical effect of such an injunction will be to force (Viacom)...(to) either divest itself of (MTV Networks) ... or withdraw from the USA joint venture" by triggering a buy/sell provision in the partnership agreement, Seagram said in an earlier court document.
In triggering the buy/sell provision, Viacom would have to sell its half of the partnership at the low end of a valuation range or buy Seagram's half at the high end.
Viacom has asked Steele to order a public auction of USA Networks, asserting that the market would provide the highest possible price.

A source close to Viacom told Reuters that the judge is not necessarily limited to contract law, and that Steele himself referred in his ruling to the court's "broad powers" in fashioning a fair or equitable remedy.

"They are seeking a remedy for something for which they have suffered no harm," the source said. "Viacom didn't engage in competition in flagrant violation of the agreement," but inherited its untenable position when it acquired Paramount.

In court papers Friday, Seagram responded that "Viacom's remedy ... completely disregards the parties' agreement and invites the court to undertake a wholesale rewriting of its exit and dissolution provisions."
Behind the legal posturing, money remains the real issue, with neither Seagram chief Edgar Bronfman Jr or Viacom Chairman Sumner Redstone willing to buy high or sell low.
Seagram has said in court papers that it needs USA Networks to stay in the cable business, even though Bronfman came close to accepting a Viacom buyout offer last fall.
It is not known when Steele will decide the issue. But both sides have made it clear that whatever his decision, the legal battles that began in April 1996 will continue on appeal.
